Figure 3:PAWlicy.A frozen Native LAM labels each video window
with one past and three future latent groups;t−1,t,…,t+3t{-}1,t,\dots,t{+}3index
temporal groups, each containing four video frames. Sharing attention with the VLM,
the latent action DiT reconstructs the past and predicts the future, and the
action DiT conditions on it to generate actions. Video without actions still
trains the latent pathway.

Figure 4:Native latent actions transfer.A latent𝐚^\hat{\mathbf{a}}is read
once from a source clip (blue) in the IDM mode of Native LAM and replayed
in its FDM mode from a different first frame (orange), which is generated
with GPT image generation from the source first frame; dotted frames are
generated. The generated videos carry out the source
motion with another embodiment, in another scene, from human to robot, and
from simulation to a photorealistic scene, although no transfer objective is used in
training.

Figure 5:Interpolating latents interpolates the motion.Latents read
from a still clip and a full-action clip are blended and replayed from the same
first frame. The top and bottom rows are the two source clips; the dotted
frames between them are generated. Each intermediate latent yields one
coherent motion that travels part of the way, further asβ\betagrows;
blending pixels instead superimposes static and moving arms (red box).

Figure 6:Frames generated from the latent
actions of different LAMs.A real-robot clip of picking up a banana and
placing it in a basket (top row) runs left to right;
the first frame is real.
(a) Frame by frame: every method, Native LAM included, is used as a
conventional LAM on frame pairs; for each two consecutive frames, it encodes
the latent action between them (IDM) and generates the second frame from the
real first one with its own world model (FDM), similar to teacher forcing.
(b) Whole clip (autoregressive): the other LAMs generate each frame from the
previouslygeneratedone with the latent action of the corresponding
pair of real frames;
Native LAM reads the whole clip at once in IDM mode and generates the
whole clip from the real first frame in one pass in FDM mode.

Figure 7:Counterfactual pairs prevent posterior collapse.A latent
action is read in IDM mode from a source clip in which the left arm grasps the
tissue (top) or from its still counterfactual, which holds the first frame
(bottom), and the FDM regenerates the clip from the same start frame with
shared prompt, noise, and seed. Circles mark the end pose of the arm. Trained
for 2k steps without counterfactual pairs, the FDM reaches for the cup in both
cases. This is posterior collapse: the FDM ignores the latent and
hallucinates a reach for the cup from the first frame alone.
With counterfactual pairs, the same 2k steps already keep the still latent still, although
the moving latent still reaches for the cup. At 13k steps the generated end
frames match the source in both cases.
